title: Ezekiel 18:21–32
context: The LORD turns to the wicked who repent and the righteous who turn away. The wicked who turns from his sins will live, and his transgressions will not be remembered. The righteous who turns to iniquity will die in it. The people complain that the way of the Lord is not fair, and the LORD answers that it is their ways that are unfair. He calls the house of Israel to return, to cast away their transgressions, and to make themselves a new heart and a new spirit, for he has no pleasure in the death of anyone. Ezekiel 33:10-20 restates much of this. Both traditions hear a sincere call to repent; they differ on how the call relates to God’s purpose and on what a righteous person’s turning away implies, and existing site discussions are noted in the verse notes.

verses.text: “But if the wicked turns from all his sins that he has committed, and keeps all my statutes, and does that which is lawful and right, he shall surely live. He shall not die.
verses.arminianNotes: But if the wicked turns from all his sins Arminian readers see a real opportunity for the wicked to turn by God’s grace and live, an offer open to every sinner.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree that the promise is sincere, and they hold that such turning is itself the fruit of grace, as the promise of a new heart in Ezekiel 36:26 suggests.

verses.text: None of his transgressions that he has committed will be remembered against him. In his righteousness that he has done, he shall live.
verses.arminianNotes: None of his transgressions that he has committed will be remembered against him. Arminian readers see the fullness of forgiveness for the one who repents, his past no longer counted.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s gracious forgetting of sin, a theme both traditions celebrate. They note the phrase in his righteousness that he has done, he shall live, read within the covenant.

verses.text: Have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked?” says the Lord GOD, “and not rather that he should return from his way, and live?
verses.arminianNotes: Have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked? Arminian readers see God’s sincere desire that every sinner should return from his way, and live; the 1 Timothy 2:4 box treats this question, and see 2 Peter 3:9.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers affirm that God takes no delight when sinners perish and that the call to return is sincere, while distinguishing his revealed desire from his decree, as the discussion at 1 Timothy 2:4 records.

verses.text: “But when the righteous turns away from his righteousness, and commits iniquity, and does according to all the abominations that the wicked man does, should he live? None of his righteous deeds that he has done will be remembered. In his trespass that he has trespassed, and in his sin that he has sinned, in them he shall die.
verses.arminianNotes: “But when the righteous turns away from his righteousness, and commits iniquity, and does according to all the abominations that the wicked man does, should he live?” Arminian readers see a real possibility that one who was truly righteous may turn to iniquity and perish. The wider question of falling away is treated at Hebrews 6:4 and Hebrews 6:6, and is not settled here.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hold either that those who finally fall away were not truly regenerate, or that the warning is a real means God uses to keep his people persevering. The wider question of falling away is treated at Hebrews 6:4 and Hebrews 6:6, and is not settled here.

verses.text: “Yet you say, ‘The way of the Lord is not equal.’ Hear now, house of Israel: Is my way not equal? Aren’t your ways unequal?
verses.arminianNotes: Is my way not equal? Arminian readers see the people accusing God of unfairness, and the LORD turning the charge back on them: their ways are unequal.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the LORD defends his justice rather than his inscrutability here. Both traditions affirm that God’s judgments are right and that the fault lies with the people.

verses.text: When the righteous man turns away from his righteousness, and commits iniquity, and dies in it, then he dies in his iniquity that he has done.
verses.arminianNotes: then he dies in his iniquity that he has done. Arminian readers see the seriousness of apostasy: a person who turned from righteousness and then died in iniquity without returning.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that many readers in both traditions see the immediate horizon as life and death in the coming judgment, while also applying the verse to final destiny. Ezekiel 33:12-13 restates the warning.

verses.text: Again, when the wicked man turns away from his wickedness that he has committed, and does that which is lawful and right, he will save his soul alive.
verses.arminianNotes: Again, when the wicked man turns away from his wickedness Arminian readers see the door of mercy open: the wicked who turns will save his soul alive.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the turning involves doing that which is lawful and right. True repentance shows itself in a changed life, a point both traditions share.

verses.text: Because he considers, and turns away from all his transgressions that he has committed, he shall surely live. He shall not die.
verses.arminianNotes: Because he considers, Arminian readers see thoughtful repentance, a turning from all his transgressions, as a real human act that God’s grace enables and invites.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the word considers, the inward reflection that precedes turning. They see God’s grace at work in such reflection, leading to the promise he shall surely live.

verses.text: Yet the house of Israel says, ‘The way of the Lord is not fair.’ House of Israel, aren’t my ways fair? Aren’t your ways unfair?
verses.arminianNotes: Yet the house of Israel says, ‘The way of the Lord is not fair.’ Arminian readers see the people’s complaint repeated, and the LORD repeating his answer: their ways are unfair.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the repetition underlines the people’s persistence in blaming God. The LORD patiently restates his case before the call to repent that follows.

verses.text: “Therefore I will judge you, house of Israel, everyone according to his ways,” says the Lord GOD. “Return, and turn yourselves from all your transgressions, so iniquity will not be your ruin.
verses.arminianNotes: Therefore I will judge you, house of Israel, everyone according to his ways, Arminian readers see judgment by individual conduct joined to an urgent call: Return, and turn yourselves.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the call to turn so iniquity will not be your ruin is sincere and pressing. Both traditions hear in it God’s genuine invitation to his people.

verses.text: Cast away from you all your transgressions in which you have transgressed; and make yourself a new heart and a new spirit. For why will you die, house of Israel?
verses.arminianNotes: Cast away from you all your transgressions in which you have transgressed; Arminian readers see the command to make yourself a new heart and a new spirit as implying a grace-enabled response; see the Deuteronomy 10:16 box.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read the command alongside the promises of Ezekiel 11:19 and 36:26, where God gives the new heart; the Deuteronomy 5:29 box treats this, and see Deuteronomy 30:6. Both hear the question that follows, For why will you die, house of Israel? as a sincere plea.

verses.text: For I have no pleasure in the death of him who dies,” says the Lord GOD. “Therefore turn yourselves, and live!
verses.arminianNotes: For I have no pleasure in the death of him who dies, Arminian readers hear the closing plea to turn and live as God’s sincere offer to all people; compare what is said at 18:23 about God’s desire in 1 Timothy 2:4.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear a sincere call, while reading it within God’s purpose to give life. Ezekiel 33:11 repeats this declaration and adds the cry, Turn, turn from your evil ways! to the call.
